8
A child of mass 20 kg stands on the rough surface of a sledge of mass 40 kg. The sledge can
slide on a horizontal frictionless surface.
One end of a rope is attached to the sledge. The rope passes around a fixed frictionless pole,
and the other end of the rope is held by the child, as shown.
horizontal rope
frictionless
pole
frictionless surface
The rope is horizontal. The child pulls on the rope with a horizontal force of 12 N. This causes the
child and the sledge to move with equal acceleration towards the pole.
What is the frictional force between the child and the sledge?
A
4.0 N
B
6.0 N
C
8.0 N
D
12 N

hints: Notice the $12\text{ N}$ tension pulls to the right in two places: on the hands of the $20\text{ kg}$ child and on the sledge where the rope is attached.

Connect the two pulls to $F = ma$: the child has $12\text{ N}$ right minus friction left, while the $40\text{ kg}$ sledge has $12\text{ N}$ right plus friction right, both with the same acceleration $a$.
First add the two $F = ma$ equations to find the common $a$ for the $60\text{ kg}$ total, then use $T - f = m a$ for the child to find $f$.
walkthrough: Treat the rope tension as $T = 12\text{ N}$ everywhere because the pole is frictionless. It pulls right on the child and right on the sledge attachment.

Let $a$ be the common acceleration toward the pole and $f$ be the magnitude of friction. Friction on the $20\text{ kg}$ child acts left, opposing the rope pull, while friction on the $40\text{ kg}$ sledge acts right by Newton's third law.
Write $F = ma$ toward the pole for each body: for the child $T - f = m a$, and for the sledge $T + f = M a$.
Add the equations to eliminate $f$: $2T = (m + M)a$. Substitute $T = 12\text{ N}$, $m + M = 60\text{ kg}$ to get $a = 24/60 = 0.40\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Use the child equation to find $f$: $f = T - m a = 12 - 20 \times 0.40 = 12 - 8.0 = 4.0\text{ N}$.

A.explanation: With $a = 0.40\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the child needs $m a = 8.0\text{ N}$ to the right, so the $12\text{ N}$ rope pull must be reduced by $4.0\text{ N}$ of friction to the left.

B.explanation: This would give the child a net force of $6.0\text{ N}$ and the sledge a net force of $18\text{ N}$, which give different accelerations for the $20\text{ kg}$ and $40\text{ kg}$ masses.

C.explanation: This is the net $m a$ force needed for the $20\text{ kg}$ child, not the friction; the friction is the difference between the $12\text{ N}$ tension and this net force.

D.explanation: If friction were $12\text{ N}$ it would cancel the $12\text{ N}$ tension on the child, giving the child zero net force and zero acceleration.
